text: When a multi-cloud proposal gets costed out, the number that gets attention is infrastructure spend on the second provider. That number is real, but it's rarely what actually breaks a multi-cloud initiative a year in. The cost that breaks it is operational — the ongoing tax of running two of almost everything, paid by the engineers and operators who keep both environments working, secure, and understood.

Start with tooling. Terraform can target more than one provider from the same workflow, which genuinely helps, but it doesn't make the providers identical. A deployment pipeline that works cleanly against one provider's APIs often needs real, separate engineering to work against the second provider's equivalent service, because equivalent rarely means identical in behavior or defaults. Multiply that across every pipeline and policy ruleset a team maintains, and duplicated tooling stops being an abstraction.

Skills are next, and they're easy to underestimate. A team running two clouds needs provider-specific depth twice, not because concepts like compute or networking differ, but because the implementation details that matter during an actual incident are provider-specific and don't transfer. That's a real hiring and training cost, and it quietly worsens the organization's bus factor unless someone deliberately invests in cross-training both teams.

Security and monitoring are where the cost is easiest to miss, because 'just configure it the same way' sounds simple and almost never is. Microsoft Entra ID and AWS IAM are built on genuinely different concepts, so a policy has to be re-thought, not re-typed. Observability faces the same choice: run two native monitoring stacks in parallel, or pay for a third-party aggregator that unifies the view at its own real licensing and integration cost.

None of this means multi-cloud is never worth it — it means pricing all four categories honestly before approval, not discovering them in year two. Put a real number on tooling, skills, security rework, and monitoring, add it to the infrastructure line item, and compare that total against what the driver is actually worth. Lesson 8 picks up from here with a pragmatic way to avoid lock-in without paying that full tax.
